analysis.one_liner: Strengthens workplace harassment protections, bans forced arbitration, and phases out the separate tipped minimum wage.
analysis.headline: Introduced with 20 Senate cosponsors and referred to the Senate HELP Committee on February 12, 2026, the bill has seen no hearings, markup, or vote since.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would tighten federal workplace discrimination law in several ways at once. Employers would have to adopt anti-harassment policies and training; workers would get more time to sue, uncapped damages, and an easier standard for proving harassment; companies could no longer force workers into private arbitration or silence them with nondisclosure agreements over discrimination claims; and the separate lower minimum wage for tipped workers — currently as low as $2.13 an hour in federal law — would be phased up to the full federal minimum. It also funds legal help for low-income workers who face discrimination.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers who experience discrimination or harassment — especially low-wage and tipped workers, who are disproportionately women — gain stronger legal tools, longer filing windows, access to court instead of forced arbitration, and funded legal help. Small employers would be newly covered and could seek help through free EEOC model policies and training materials.

how_it_helps.text: Employers with 15 or more employees would be required to adopt comprehensive anti-harassment policies, disseminate them annually, and provide interactive training, with fines of up to $1,000 per violation ($5,000 for repeat or willful violations).

The bill writes a statutory harassment standard under which a single incident can qualify, incidents are judged in total rather than one by one, and power differences, slurs, and threats are counted as factors.

It would drop the minimum number of covered employees from 15 to 1, extend protection to independent contractors, interns, and volunteers, remove the caps on compensatory and punitive damages, extend statutes of limitations, and let workers show discrimination was a motivating factor even when other factors also played a role.
It would prohibit mandatory arbitration of discrimination claims and restrict nondisclosure agreements, letting workers take claims to court and speak publicly.

The federal tipped minimum wage would rise from its current low base to $3.60 in the first year and then step up yearly by $1.50 until it equals the full federal minimum wage, after which the separate tipped wage is repealed.

It would fund grants for civil legal assistance for low-income workers and for state-based worker advocacy systems, and authorize a national survey measuring how often workplace harassment actually occurs.

analysis.who_pays: Employers bear the direct cost: restaurants would pay tipped staff the full minimum wage, companies would pay for policies and training, and businesses that rely on forced arbitration and nondisclosure agreements would lose those legal shields. Critics also warn that uncapped damages and broader employer coverage could raise litigation exposure and insurance costs, with the heaviest relative burden on small businesses.

drawbacks.text: Extending coverage to every employer with even one employee (Sec. 202) and requiring policies and training would impose compliance costs that fall hardest on the smallest businesses, even though the bill directs the EEOC to provide free model materials to firms under 15 employees.

Removing the statutory caps on compensatory and punitive damages (Sec. 203) and allowing a single incident to support a harassment claim (Sec. 204) would expose employers to larger jury awards and more litigation, which supporters of the current caps argue raises insurance costs and can chill hiring.

The tipped-wage phase-out could cut some tipped employees' take-home pay in practice if employers offset higher cash wages by reducing scheduling or shifting duties, the concern the restaurant industry raises against tip-credit repeal; the bill responds by guaranteeing employees the right to keep their tips.
Banning mandatory arbitration of discrimination claims (Sec. 303) would remove a faster, cheaper private dispute channel that employers and some workers prefer, pushing more cases into court.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The worker-side gains are substantial and concrete: longer filing windows, no forced arbitration, uncapped damages for severe cases, and a path to the full minimum wage for tipped workers, most of whom are women. The costs are real but mostly bounded — training and policy compliance is a modest per-employee burden, and the biggest cost shifts (tipped wages, arbitration) fall on specific industries that today capture the savings. The design is more debatable on uncapped damages and one-employee coverage, where honest supporters would acknowledge higher litigation exposure for small firms.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee on the day it was introduced and has had no hearing, markup, or floor vote since.

narrative.text: Senator Patty Murray introduced S. 3865, the BE HEARD in the Workplace Act, on February 12, 2026, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions the same day.
The bill has 20 cosponsors — 19 of the Senate's 45 Democrats and one Independent — with no Republican support listed.
The action history shows no activity beyond introduction and committee referral: no hearings, no committee vote, and no floor action.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers are better off for now: restaurants keep the lower tipped minimum wage, companies keep mandatory arbitration and the use of nondisclosure agreements in discrimination cases, and no employer faces the new training, policy, or expanded-liability requirements.

against.what_they_did: Long-running public campaigns against tip-credit repeal and forced-arbitration bans of the kind this bill contains.

sides.party_line_note: All 20 cosponsors are Democrats or Independents, with no Republican support listed, and Republicans hold 55 of 100 Senate seats plus the committee chairmanship that controls the bill's path.

industries.industry: Restaurants and other employers of tipped workers
industries.note: The bill phases out the separate tipped minimum wage — which can be as low as $2.13 an hour — by raising the cash wage yearly until it equals the full federal minimum, while guaranteeing workers keep their tips. The industry has historically fought tip-credit repeal on the argument that it raises labor costs and can cut hours.

industries.industry: Employers that require arbitration of workplace disputes
industries.note: The bill bans mandatory arbitration of discrimination claims and limits related nondisclosure agreements, ending a system that keeps harassment cases out of court and largely out of public view.

Dropping the coverage threshold from 15 employees to 1 brings the smallest businesses under federal discrimination law for the first time, but the EEOC must give them free model policies and training materials to ease compliance.
The bill funds grants for civil legal assistance for low-income workers and state advocacy systems, and broader, uncapped claims mean more cases for the employment bar.
Mandatory anti-harassment policies and interactive training for employers with 15 or more employees would create demand for training services, alongside the free EEOC materials.

analysis.trajectory: With no committee action more than a year into the session, no Republican cosponsors, and a majority party that controls both the committee calendar and the floor, the bill is very unlikely to advance in this Congress. Prior versions of this proposal and similar measures have also died in committee without a vote.
